units.passage: In the investigation and resolution of allegations of student academic dishonesty and student misconduct, the Department’s actions are intended to be corrective, educationally sound, fundamentally fair, and based on reliable evidence.
units.why: Actions are "based on reliable evidence", a standard for findings of dishonesty (P69).
units.fit_note: The standard is stated generally, without saying what counts as reliable.

units.passage: cannot serve as sole evidence in a misconduct case
units.policy: AI detection tools cannot serve as sole evidence in a misconduct case.
units.why: Detectors 'cannot serve as sole evidence in a misconduct case', a limit on what proves misuse (P69).

units.passage: A high AI probability score can encourage additional scrutiny but does not definitively prove a student used AI on an assignment.
units.why: 'A high AI probability score can encourage additional scrutiny but does not definitively prove a student used AI': an evidence standard, P69.

units.passage: Faculty should not conflate code similarity findings with AI detection findings. Whether code is similar to another submission and whether a student used AI are separate questions.
units.why: 'Faculty should not conflate code similarity findings with AI detection findings': an evidence rule, P69.

units.passage: Faculty building a misconduct case should document behavioral evidence: writing or coding style inconsistent with prior submissions, responses that do not address the actual prompt, fabricated facts, fictitious references, word counts or styles inconsistent with assignment guidelines, or direct similarity to AI output when the prompt is entered into a model.
units.why: 'Faculty building a misconduct case should document behavioral evidence: writing or coding style inconsistent with prior submissions ...': P69.

units.passage: Signs of AI-generated content can include inconsistencies in writing style, overly generic or formulaic responses, or a mismatch between a student's typical work and their submission.
units.why: Lists the kinds of evidence to weigh ('inconsistencies in writing style... mismatch'), which is P69 (evidence kinds); P40 is for tools and logs, which this is not.
units.fit_note: Lists signs of AI-generated work rather than a standard of proof.

units.passage: Identical, or nearly identical, submissions will be considered conclusive evidence of plagiarism.
units.why: 'Identical, or nearly identical, submissions will be considered conclusive evidence of plagiarism' sets what counts as proof of misuse, P69. It follows the generative-AI detection sentence in the same paragraph, but does not itself name AI.
units.fit_note: Applies to identical submissions generally; AI is not named in this sentence.

units.passage: ECE faculty may compare your writing style obtained in an in-person writing assignment to the one in the suspected assignment
units.why: Faculty may compare writing style with an in-person sample, a kind of evidence in a misuse finding (P69).
units.fit_note: Names a specific evidence method (writing-style comparison). | Evidence is writing-style comparison by instructors, not software or logs.

units.passage: Note that fake citations, references that do not actually exist or are not relevant to the assignment, or other forms of hallucinations will be considered as evidence of AI-generated content
units.why: "fake citations, references that do not actually exist ... will be considered as evidence of AI-generated content" sets hallucinated references as evidence of AI use: P69.
units.fit_note: Names one kind of evidence; no standard of proof.

units.passage: The evaluation of an AI detection tool alone is not sufficient evidence to conclude thata student has violated any rules.
units.why: 'The evaluation of an AI detection tool alone is not sufficient evidence to conclude that a student has violated any rules' sets an evidence standard for misuse (P69), not just that detectors are unreliable (P39).

units.passage: Suspected use of Generative AI in coursework is not sufficient evidence to begin a formal Academic Integrity investigation.
units.why: "Suspected use ... is not sufficient evidence to begin a formal Academic Integrity investigation" sets an evidence standard, P69.

units.passage: Look for unusual consistency in tone or style, especially if it deviates from a student’s previous work. AI-generated text may also include overly generic or repetitive phrases, lack of deep analysis, or produce content that appears superficially polished but lacks the nuanced understanding expected from human authors.
units.why: The list of signs ('unusual consistency in tone or style', 'overly generic or repetitive phrases') names kinds of evidence to weigh when judging AI misuse, which is P69; it is not P40 because no tool is involved.
units.fit_note: Lists indicators of AI use (generic phrasing, lack of analysis, too-advanced work) rather than a standard of proof. Also states the kinds of evidence to weigh (style, generic phrasing, unexplained errors) but no standard of proof.

units.passage: However, it’s important to use these tools as part of a broader assessment rather than relying on them exclusively. Combine them with your own judgment and knowledge of your students’ work to make a well-informed decision.
units.policy: Detection tools are used as part of a broader assessment, not relied on exclusively, and combined with the instructor's judgment and knowledge of students' work.
units.why: 'use these tools as part of a broader assessment rather than relying on them exclusively' says detector output is supporting evidence only, matching the broadened P69 (not P39, which says detectors are unreliable or not used).

units.passage: Be sure to include any samples of earlier/baseline student writing to which the writing in question can be compared.
units.why: The memo tells instructors to 'include any samples of earlier/baseline student writing to which the writing in question can be compared' when reporting suspected misuse. That says what evidence supports an AI-misuse report, so P69 (evidence for misuse findings) fits; P40 (tools and logs used to identify misuse) fits less well because no tool or log is named. Instructor, when-misuse, should.
units.fit_note: Names earlier/baseline student writing as the comparison evidence to attach to an incident report; the type is about evidence standards for finding misuse. (Coder A used P40, noting it names baseline writing samples attached to an incident report rather than similarity checks and logs.)

units.passage: Clearly limit allowable methods, tools, or references, and specify that deviations from these restrictions could constitute evidence of potential integrity violations.
units.why: It adds to 'specify that deviations from these restrictions could constitute evidence of potential integrity violations'. This sets that deviation counts as evidence, so P69.
units.fit_note: Tells students in advance what will count as evidence.

units.passage: Violation Awareness Inquire About Unusual Submissions Instructors should use their initial impressions of potential violations involving generative AI as a starting point for deeper inquiry, supported by objective and verifiable evidence, before proceeding with academic integrity hearings.
units.why: The page says instructors 'should use their initial impressions of potential violations involving generative AI as a starting point for deeper inquiry, supported by objective and verifiable evidence'. Evidence must support a charge, so P69.

units.passage: Evidence of Violation Gather Objective Evidence Faculty should follow up their initial concerns about a generative AI-related violation with tangible evidence, such as: Submitted work includes citations or references to content that does not exist or cannot be verified.
units.why: Faculty 'should follow up ... with tangible evidence' such as nonexistent citations, advanced methods, inability to explain the work, or inconsistency with drafts; kinds of evidence to weigh: P69.

units.passage: Submitted work includes citations or references to content that does not exist or cannot be verified.
units.why: An example of evidence: work 'includes citations or references to content that does not exist or cannot be verified'. A kind of evidence, so P69.

units.passage: Inclusion of advanced references, methods, or approaches that exceed the scope of the course or seem implausible without external assistance.
units.why: Another example is 'advanced references, methods, or approaches that exceed the scope of the course'. A kind of evidence, so P69.

units.passage: The student is unable to verbally explain, expand upon, or defend their submitted work when queried.
units.why: Another example is 'The student is unable to verbally explain, expand upon, or defend their submitted work when queried.' A kind of evidence, so P69.

units.passage: The work is inconsistent with previously submitted work or preparatory steps submitted by the student, such as outlines, drafts, or prior discussions during office hours.
units.why: Another example is work 'inconsistent with previously submitted work or preparatory steps'. A kind of evidence, so P69.

units.passage: Evidence of an academic integrity violation needs to meet a clear and convincing standard.
units.why: The page says evidence 'needs to meet a clear and convincing standard', explained as above 'more likely than not' and below 'beyond a reasonable doubt'. A standard of proof, so P69.

units.passage: It is important that Turnitin scores not be used as a definitive measure of misconduct. Instructors should review sentence-level data from Turnitin and determine the appropriate next steps.
units.why: 'It is important that Turnitin scores not be used as a definitive measure of misconduct' says the detector cannot serve as proof (P39).

units.passage: If you suspect a piece of work was completed using generative AI, carefully analyze the work and compare it to past student writing.
units.why: "carefully analyze the work and compare it to past student writing" tells instructors what other evidence to weigh when AI use is suspected, so P69.

units.passage: They still have a place, but they provide information, not indictments. Instructor time is far better spent on helping students use AI responsibly than on trying to forbid AI in the learning process.
units.why: 'They still have a place, but they provide information, not indictments' allows detectors only as supporting evidence, P69.

units.passage: What is proof of AI use? How will you decide when and whether to pursue an academic misconduct case?
units.why: "What is proof of AI use?" asks instructors to decide beforehand what counts as proof, evidence standards, P69.
units.fit_note: poses questions to settle in advance rather than stating a standard. | Poses the question for instructors to answer in advance; sets no standard.

units.passage: Outputs from these tools should never serve as the sole basis for an academic integrity decision.
units.why: "Outputs from these tools should never serve as the sole basis for an academic integrity decision": detector output is not enough evidence, P69.

units.passage: Results from AI detection tools should be treated only as potential indicators of misconduct, not definitive proof. These results should not serve as the sole basis for grading decisions.
units.why: Detector results are "only potential indicators of misconduct, not definitive proof". Evidence standard, P69.

units.passage: These results should not serve as the sole basis for grading decisions.
units.why: Detector results may not be the sole basis for grading, an evidence standard, P69.

units.passage: While information from these tools may be included in referrals to academic deans, such information alone will not solely determine a student’s responsibility.
units.why: Detector information in a dean referral "alone will not solely determine a student's responsibility". Evidence standard, P69.

units.passage: Results from GenAI detection tools should be treated only as potential indicators of misconduct, not definitive proof.
units.why: Detector results 'should be treated only as potential indicators of misconduct, not definitive proof'. Detector output is supporting evidence only, P69.

units.passage: These results should not serve as the sole basis for grading decisions.
units.why: Detector results 'should not serve as the sole basis for grading decisions'. A limit on evidence, P69.

units.passage: While information from these tools may be included in referrals to the Office of Student Conduct, such information alone will not solely determine a student's responsibility.
units.why: Detector information in referrals 'alone will not solely determine a student's responsibility'. Evidence standard for the conduct process, P69.

units.passage: While there may be cases of genuine misunderstanding, if there is a misunderstanding so egregious that common sense would indicate a different course of action, instructors may choose to pursue academic sanctions within the academic integrity process.
units.why: "if there is a misunderstanding so egregious that common sense would indicate a different course of action, instructors may choose to pursue academic sanctions": sets a threshold for sanctioning despite misunderstanding, nearest P69.
units.fit_note: Sets a threshold for sanctioning despite misunderstanding rather than a proof standard.

units.passage: Will not assign a grade on the basis of suspicion.
units.why: "Will not assign a grade on the basis of suspicion": a limit on sanctions requiring more than suspicion, an evidence standard, P69.

units.passage: If you're concerned about the authenticity of student content, always apply critical thinking, check the source, and if possible, verify information through multiple channels
units.why: "always apply critical thinking, check the source, and if possible, verify information through multiple channels" tells instructors how to weigh evidence of authenticity (P69).

units.passage: A finding of misconduct must be based on a preponderance of the credible evidence.
units.why: "A finding of misconduct must be based on a preponderance of the credible evidence" sets the standard of proof (P69).

units.passage: Given the unreliability of these tools and the risk of false results, we do not recommend using these detection tools as the single piece of evidence to support a violation of the academic integrity policy.
units.why: "we do not recommend using these detection tools as the single piece of evidence to support a violation" makes detector output only supporting evidence, which is P69 (evidence standards); P39 says detectors are not relied on at all.

units.passage: these tools are unreliable and should not be used as sole evidence of misconduct
units.why: 'unreliable and should not be used as sole evidence of misconduct' limits detector output to supporting evidence, which P69 covers (broadened).

units.passage: Detection results are not admissible proof of academic dishonesty.
units.why: "Not admissible proof" sets an evidence standard for misuse findings: P69, chosen over P39 as it says what counts as proof.

units.passage: Conversations and context matter
units.why: 'Conversations and context matter more than software scores' sets what evidence to weigh, P69.

units.passage: Reminder: Suspicion alone is not proof.
units.why: 'Suspicion alone is not proof' sets an evidence standard (P69).

units.passage: Misconduct investigations and official sanctions should be reserved for clear violations.
units.why: 'Misconduct investigations and official sanctions should be reserved for clear violations' sets a threshold for formal action (P69).
units.fit_note: A threshold for escalating, which also favors educative responses. A threshold on when to investigate, not about the kind of evidence.

units.passage: When submitting an academic misconduct report, you will want to include any evidence you have.
units.why: 'you will want to include any evidence you have' in a misconduct report sets the standard of submitting evidence, P69.

units.passage: this is straightforward – for example, if the student accidentally included the prompt they used or language from the AI tool like “Can I help you with anything else?” at the end
units.why: Examples of clear evidence, such as the prompt left in the text or 'Can I help you with anything else?', say what proves AI use, P69.

units.passage: Instead, the best evidence often comes from the intuition you have as an instructor. Some things that might indicate inappropriate AI use include:
units.why: 'the best evidence often comes from the intuition you have as an instructor' with listed signs sets what evidence to weigh, P69.
units.fit_note: P69 includes statements that hunches are not enough; this page treats instructor intuition as the best evidence.

units.passage: Language too advanced or specialized for the nature of the assignment
units.why: 'Language too advanced or specialized for the nature of the assignment' is a listed sign of AI use, P69.

units.passage: Using obscure, irrelevant, or non-existent references . Checking for this can be supported by requiring students to include a direct link to all references.
units.why: 'Using obscure, irrelevant, or non-existent references' is a listed sign, with the advice to require 'a direct link to all references', P69.

units.passage: A writing style that significantly differs from other work submitted in class.
units.why: 'A writing style that significantly differs from other work submitted in class' is a listed sign, P69.

units.passage: Checking for this can be supported by requiring students to include a direct link to all references. A writing style that significantly differs from other work submitted in class. Detecting this can be helped by collecting an in-person writing sample early in the semester. The student admitting to AI use. In many cases, if you meet with the student and have an attitude of genuine support, the student will admit to inappropriate AI use. Academic Integrity Assistance If you have additional questions about the academic misconduct process or how to handle a specific case that you are encountering, please contact the Office of Student Conduct & Community Standards : 402-472-2021 or studentconduct@unl.edu . If you have any feedback about the content of this page or ideas for additional content to include, please reach out to the page developer Amy Ort ( aort@unl.edu ).
units.why: 'The student admitting to AI use' counts as evidence, P69.

units.passage: Due to the unreliability and bias of AI detection tools , using these tools to identify violations of academic integrity should be a starting point for discussion, not as conclusive evidence.
units.why: 'a starting point for discussion, not as conclusive evidence' limits detector output to supporting evidence, P69 (broadened) rather than P39 which is the reliability claim.
units.fit_note: Detector may still be used to start a conversation; P39 says detectors are not relied on.

units.passage: All investigations into academic integrity should not rely solely on one accountability measurement
units.why: 'should not rely solely on one accountability measurement' is an evidence standard for misuse findings, P69.

units.passage: An AI detection tool must not be the sole source of information that leads to discipline
units.policy: An AI detection tool must not be the sole source of information that leads to discipline
units.why: "An AI detection tool must not be the sole source of information that leads to discipline" sets an evidence standard for findings, P69.

units.passage: AI detection tools cannot be relied upon as conclusive evidence of improper AI use by a student
units.policy: AI detection tools cannot be relied upon as conclusive evidence of improper AI use by a student
units.why: "cannot be relied upon as conclusive evidence of improper AI use by a student" is an evidence rule on detectors, P69.

units.passage: it cannot serve as the sole basis for a finding of academic misconduct
units.why: "it cannot serve as the sole basis for a finding of academic misconduct" is an evidence standard, P69.

units.passage: They should not be used to make definitive judgments about academic integrity
units.why: Detector output 'should not be used to make definitive judgments' on integrity, i.e. at most supporting evidence, which the broadened P69 covers; P39 fits less because it concerns unreliability, not the evidence standard.

units.passage: I will use submitted coursework, assignment directions, conversations with you about your work and process, and this syllabus to determine whether academic misconduct occurred.
units.why: Lists what evidence the instructor weighs ('submitted coursework, ... conversations with you about your work and process'), an evidence standard (P69); it also mentions talking with the student.

units.passage: In cases in which students have not been informed about acceptable generative AI use within a course, it becomes difficult to establish academic dishonesty.
units.why: When students were not told the rules 'it becomes difficult to establish academic dishonesty'; an evidence standard tied to notice, P69.
units.fit_note: States what follows when no AI rule was communicated (misconduct is hard to establish) rather than a fixed standard of evidence.

units.passage: Any academic consequences should be based on clear evidence and documented justification.
units.why: "Any academic consequences should be based on clear evidence and documented justification" sets an evidence standard, P69.

units.passage: Instructors in the writing program try to distinguish between inadvertent and deliberate plagiarism, as well as whether and how AI has been used in the writing process.
units.why: NDSU Center for Writers example: instructors 'try to distinguish between inadvertent and deliberate plagiarism, as well as whether and how AI has been used'; an evidentiary distinction, P69.
units.fit_note: Distinguishes kinds of misuse and intent rather than setting an evidence standard.

units.passage: We can also look for evidence of engaging in the writing process – i.e. engaging in revision and reflecting on revision choices. We can also consider the student’s level of engagement in the class.
units.why: Instructors can compare against the student's other work and look for 'evidence of engaging in the writing process', naming kinds of evidence to weigh, so P69.

units.passage: A report should be filed if an instructor decides that a preponderance of evidence shows the student violated the policy.
units.why: The threshold "a preponderance of evidence shows the student violated the policy" is a standard of proof for filing a report, hence P69.
units.fit_note: The standard is stated for all integrity violations, not AI specifically.

units.passage: Due to the rapidly evolving nature of AI technologies and the inadequacy of detection tools, a detection report alone (such as Turnitin) is not sufficient evidence for a violation of the university’s academic integrity policy.
units.why: "A detection report alone (such as Turnitin) is not sufficient evidence for a violation" limits detector output to supporting evidence, which is the broadened P69.

units.passage: Be cognizant that results such detectors produce cannot be considered as definitive evidence of an academic integrity violation.
units.why: Detector results "cannot be considered as definitive evidence of an academic integrity violation" sets what is not enough proof of misuse, so P69 rather than P39; introduced by 'Be cognizant', so advisory (should-not).

units.passage: While these tools can help point out certain identifiers of AI usage, their results alone cannot constitute a preponderance of evidence that AI was misused. It is important not to overstate their reliability.
units.policy: Detection tool results alone cannot constitute a preponderance of evidence that AI was misused.
units.why: The text says detector results 'alone cannot constitute a preponderance of evidence that AI was misused'. That sets an evidence standard for misuse findings, P69; it also limits reliance on detectors (P39 states unreliability separately).

units.passage: However, be cautious when confronting improvements in performance through a course, as improvement is of course a desirable outcome of good teaching and good efforts to learn.
units.policy: Faculty be cautious when confronting improvements in performance through a course, as improvement is a desirable outcome of good teaching and good efforts to learn.
units.why: It cautions faculty to be 'cautious when confronting improvements in performance', because improvement is desirable. This limits what counts as evidence of misuse, which is P69.

units.passage: The AI Checker percentage will be considered with all other evidence to determine if there was a violation.
units.why: 'The AI Checker percentage will be considered with all other evidence to determine if there was a violation' sets how detector output is weighed in findings (P69).

units.passage: OSAAI uses the preponderance of the evidence as the standard of evidence when making decisions in academic integrity cases.
units.why: "OSAAI uses the preponderance of the evidence as the standard of evidence" sets the proof standard for integrity cases including AI cases: P69.
units.fit_note: General standard of proof for all integrity cases; AI is not named.

units.passage: Learn about the subtle clues that can indicate AI-generated content, such as unusual phrasing or lack of context, and provide specific examples where possible.
units.why: Advice to identify AI content via 'subtle clues ... such as unusual phrasing or lack of context' proposes human cues as evidence (P69, evidence kinds).
units.fit_note: Suggests stylistic cues as indicators, in tension with later cautions. / Stylistic clues like unusual phrasing, not software or process evidence.

units.passage: If you suspect academic dishonesty based on these tools, please review, and investigate before taking disciplinary action.
units.why: 'If you suspect academic dishonesty based on these tools, please review, and investigate before taking disciplinary action' (P69 weigh evidence; P57 talking with the student is not stated).
units.fit_note: Calls for investigation before discipline, without naming a standard of proof. / Asks for investigation before discipline but sets no standard of proof.

units.passage: Student Conduct states that "online AI detection tools like Turnitin.com or GPTZero may not be effective and can result in false positives. If you choose to utilize these tools, please note that [...] we would not consider the percentages provided by these tools as dispositive on their own
units.policy: The conduct office does not consider detector percentages dispositive on their own
units.why: "we would not consider the percentages provided by these tools as dispositive on their own" sets a standard that detector scores are not sufficient evidence, P69.

units.passage: If you choose to utilize these tools, please note that while they can be suggestive of academic misconduct, we would not consider the percentages provided by these tools as dispositive on their own.
units.why: "we would not consider the percentages provided by these tools as dispositive on their own" is an evidence standard for detector output (P69).

units.passage: However, without any additional information or an acknowledgement from the student that they used a generative AI tool, there may not be enough to find that they engaged in a violation of the Code.
units.why: "without any additional information or an acknowledgement from the student ... there may not be enough to find that they engaged in a violation" sets what evidence is needed for a finding, P69.

units.passage: When an educator believes, for reasons beyond mere suspicion, that a student has attempted to violate or has violated a course academic integrity policy or assessment instruction in a way that (would have) affected the quality of the academic work, then they should submit an academic integrity claim
units.why: Sets an evidence threshold for filing a claim, 'beyond mere suspicion' (P69). The page covers AI in the same context but this sentence is general.
units.fit_note: General integrity standard, not AI-specific.

units.passage: If the committee believes they have a clear indication of both sides of the situation from the documentation provided, they will proceed with the review and decision based only on the written statements and documentation.
units.why: The committee decides 'based only on the written statements and documentation' and does not investigate, an evidence standard for findings (P69).
units.fit_note: Describes the committee's evidence basis; not AI-specific.

units.passage: carefully review suspected cases with due diligence and according to a procedure clearly explained to students on the syllabus
units.why: Instructors should 'carefully review suspected cases with due diligence and according to a procedure clearly explained to students', which sets a standard of care in finding misuse (P69) and a requirement to explain the procedure in advance.
units.fit_note: Due diligence plus a procedure explained on the syllabus; no explicit evidence standard.

units.passage: It is especially important, given the high false positive rates of current AI detection tools, that a positive result from one of these tools is not the sole determining factor of an academic integrity violation and subsequent consequences
units.why: 'a positive result from one of these tools is not the sole determining factor of an academic integrity violation' sets what evidence suffices, so P69.

units.passage: After reviewing the situation and speaking with others who might be involved or have knowledge of the situation, the instructor will determine the nature and extent of the violation, if any, by the accused student.
units.why: The passage has the instructor review the situation and speak 'with others who might be involved or have knowledge of the situation' before determining the violation, which sets how a finding is reached; nearest type is P69 though no standard of proof is given.
units.fit_note: Describes steps for gathering evidence but states no standard or kinds of evidence insufficient.

units.passage: Professors can submit reasonable suspicions based on factors such as the style and/or major differences from the given prompt

units.passage: A. If you feel as though you do not have sufficient evidence to submit an accusation, you may wait till another assignment provides sufficient evidence.
units.policy: If a professor feels there is not sufficient evidence to submit an accusation, the professor may wait till another assignment provides sufficient evidence.

units.passage: For this reason, results from these detectors will not be considered as evidence for a Rowan Report of an Academic Integrity Violation but other forms of evidence may be used to make a report.
units.why: A standard of evidence: detector results 'will not be considered as evidence' while 'other forms of evidence may be used'. It sets what counts as evidence (P69, which lists Rowan).

units.passage: For this reason, results from these detectors will not be considered as evidence for a Rowan Report of an Academic Integrity Violation but other forms of evidence may be used to make a report

units.passage: Evaluate their references carefully because fabrication is a form of academic dishonesty, faculty can submit Academic Integrity Violations based on invented sources and/or quotations

units.passage: AI detection reports generated by tools such as Turnitin can therefore only be considered alongside other evidence. They cannot serve as the sole basis for imposing an academic sanction.

units.passage: Other evidence may include documentation that the submitted assignment represents a significant or noteworthy change from the student’s previous work or that the submitted assignment is not consistent with the materials taught in the class.
units.why: Lists what 'Other evidence may include': a significant change from the student's previous work or inconsistency with class materials, i.e. kinds of evidence to weigh (P69).

units.passage: Like all reported alleged violations of the Honor Code student behavior and assignment submissions are reviewed by the Office of Student Conduct and Academic Integrity to find whether it is more likely than not- by a preponderance of the evidence that the student's behavior or work violates one or more of the Honor Code's policies.

units.passage: Large portions of text that have been copied and pasted for example could be cause for concern if the information copied and pasted is not cited or appears to be information generated elsewhere to be passed off as the student's work.

units.passage: This is not a certain means to prove a student used artificial intelligence in their work but, it does provide a line of questions to get to a more certain finding either for or against a violation of the Honor Code.

units.passage: No single indicator proves AI use.
units.why: "No single indicator proves AI use" sets an evidence standard for AI-misuse findings, P69.

units.passage: Fluent writing with limited depth, original insight or disciplinary specificity.
units.policy: Signs that work may be AI-generated include fluent writing with limited depth, generic structure and language, missing, incorrect or fabricated citations, and confident inaccuracies.
units.why: "Fluent writing with limited depth, original insight or disciplinary specificity" lists a sign of AI content, which is evidence the instructor may weigh, so P69.
units.fit_note: Describes reading-based indicators of AI text, not software, commit history or logs. | Lists a sign to weigh (overly polished but shallow responses), not a standard of proof.

units.passage: Formatting commonly found in GenAI output (e.g., lines between sections, bolded text throughout, etc.).
units.why: "Formatting commonly found in GenAI output" lists structural signs of AI content, so P69.
units.fit_note: Lists a sign to weigh (generic structure and language), not a standard of proof.

units.passage: Missing, incorrect or fabricated citations.
units.why: "Missing, incorrect or fabricated citations" is listed as a sign of AI content, so P69.
units.fit_note: Lists a sign to weigh (lack of engagement with course materials), not a standard of proof.

units.passage: Errors that reflect common AI misunderstandings rather than novice human reasoning.
units.why: "Errors that reflect common AI misunderstandings rather than novice human reasoning" is listed as a sign of AI content, so P69.
units.fit_note: Lists a sign to weigh (confident inaccuracies), not a standard of proof.

units.passage: If AI detection tools are used and suggest one’s work was produced using AI, that should be the start of data gathering and not the end decision making tool
units.why: Detector output "should be the start of data gathering and not the end decision making tool": detector results are only supporting evidence, P69.

units.passage: Data gathering could include: obvious mistakes in the written work, references that are made -up or not actually relevant to the content, writing that is not responsive to the prompt, writing that is not in keeping with past writing of the individual, etc
units.why: "Data gathering could include: obvious mistakes in the written work, references that are made-up..." lists the kinds of evidence to weigh, P69.

units.passage: Notwithstanding the foregoing, under no circumstances shall the results of AI detection tools be the single measure for determining the academic performance of or misconduct by a Student.
units.why: 'under no circumstances' may detector results be the single measure of performance or misconduct: detector output is not sufficient evidence, P69.

units.passage: AI detection results should not be the sole determinant of academic dishonesty.
units.why: 'AI detection results should not be the sole determinant of academic dishonesty' says detector output is not enough evidence alone, an evidence standard (P69) in the broadened sense.

units.passage: This ensures a fair and consistent approach to addressing concerns, relying on evidence-based evaluations and open communication with students rather than depending solely on AI detection results
units.why: 'relying on evidence-based evaluations and open communication with students rather than depending solely on AI detection results' sets an evidence standard, so P69.

units.passage: For that reason, the score cannot be the sole evidence of academic misconduct when submitting an Honor Code violation.
units.why: "The score cannot be the sole evidence of academic misconduct." It sets an evidence standard: the detector score alone is not enough, P69.

units.passage: The submission does not meet the assignment requirements or use concepts addressed within the course content.
units.why: A sign to weigh is that "the submission does not meet the assignment requirements or use concepts addressed within the course content". This is a kind of evidence for misuse, P69.

units.passage: The submission has obvious signs of AI use (hallucinations, reference to the use of a large language model, etc.).
units.why: A sign to weigh is "obvious signs of AI use (hallucinations, reference to the use of a large language model, etc.)". It is a kind of evidence for misuse, P69.

units.passage: The quality of the submission is inconsistent with other work produced by the student.
units.why: A sign to weigh is that "the quality of the submission is inconsistent with other work produced by the student". It lists what evidence to weigh, P69.
units.fit_note: The page lists this as a sign to examine, not as proof.

units.passage: If you suspect that a student has used an unauthorized resource on an assignment or assessment, you may find this blog on collecting evidence for an AI academic integrity case helpful.
units.why: "you may find this blog on collecting evidence for an AI academic integrity case helpful" points faculty with suspected misuse to evidence-collection advice; it states no standard, so informs / when-misuse / P69 with a fit note.
units.fit_note: Refers to outside guidance on collecting evidence rather than stating an evidence standard.

units.passage: If, after our conversation, I conclude it’s more likely than not that you did not personally complete an assignment you submitted under your name, I may report a violation to the campus Office of Academic Integrity & Student Conduct.
units.why: 'more likely than not' sets a standard of proof for finding the student did not do the work, an evidence standard (P69).
units.fit_note: Gives a preponderance standard for concluding a student did not do the work, rather than a rule about what evidence counts.

units.passage: such tools should not be relied on as presumptive of the use of generative AI in completing an assignment
units.policy: Generative AI detection tools should not be relied on as presumptive of the use of generative AI in completing an assignment.
units.why: 'such tools should not be relied on as presumptive of the use of generative AI' sets an evidence standard: detector output is not presumptive proof, which fits P69 (detector output not proof) better than P39 because it speaks to what counts as evidence.

units.passage: AI detection tools may help identify content potentially generated by AI, but they are not definitive and should never be used as the sole basis for academic misconduct decisions.
units.why: Says detectors "are not definitive" and must never be the "sole basis" for misconduct decisions. It is the evidence-standard rule (P69) rather than declining to use detectors (P39).

units.passage: It is important to review originality reports carefully, as similarity percentages may include properly cited sources and reference lists and do not automatically indicate plagiarism.
units.why: Warns that similarity scores do not equal plagiarism, so reports must be read carefully: evidence standards (P69).

units.passage: Turnitin also offers an AI writing assessment to help identify text that may be AI-generated; however, these results are not always accurate and should not be used as the sole basis for academic misconduct decisions.
units.why: "these results are not always accurate and should not be used as the sole basis for academic misconduct decisions" sets the evidence standard for a misconduct finding that rests on Turnitin's AI score, so P69, instructor, when-misuse, should-not.

units.passage: However, there are certain red flags that can indicate that a student may have used generative AI when completing an assignment.
units.why: "certain red flags that can indicate that a student may have used generative AI" followed by a list (inaccuracies, tone, citations, dead links) names kinds of evidence to weigh; P69.
units.fit_note: Offers indicators rather than a standard of proof. Lists manual red flags (inaccuracies, tone, fake links, unavailable sources) rather than software or logs.

units.passage: Because generative AI tools frequently generate inaccurate information, a text with multiple errors or flagrant inaccuracies may be a sign that a student has used generative AI.
units.why: "Because generative AI tools frequently generate inaccurate information, a text with multiple errors or flagrant inaccuracies may be a sign" names AI-typical errors as evidence; P69.

units.passage: If a text reads as though it were written by a machine, this is a possible red flag. Compare to previous work. A major change in tone and style from previous writings could indicate that a student has used generative AI. Assess citations. Generative AI tools may cite journal articles, book chapters, and other academic sources that are not readily available to students.
units.why: "Compare to previous work. A major change in tone and style from previous writings could indicate" use is a specific evidence type (comparison with prior work); P69.

units.passage: While a single inaccuracy or a slight change in style may not necessarily mean that a student has used generative AI, repeated or egregious instances of the aforementioned red flags may indicate that a student has used generative AI tools.
units.why: "a single inaccuracy or a slight change in style may not necessarily mean that a student has used generative AI" sets a limit on inference from red flags: single signs are not enough; P69.

units.passage: Please note that current guidelines indicate that a report to the Undergraduate Honor Council cannot be based solely on an artificial intelligence detector score.
units.why: "a report to the Undergraduate Honor Council cannot be based solely on an artificial intelligence detector score" bars detector score as sole basis; P69 (evidence standard, broadened for detector output).

units.passage: Additionally, reports of unauthorized AI use to the Undergraduate Honor Council must meet the following standards:
units.why: Reports "must meet the following standards" including alignment with the Academic Affairs policy and supporting factors such as fake links or style inconsistency; a required evidentiary standard, P69.

units.passage: the Honor Council will ultimately ask the question “is it more likely than not that this student gave and/or received unauthorized aid in some form on the assignment?”
units.policy: The Undergraduate Honor Council asks whether it is more likely than not that the student gave or received unauthorized aid on the assignment; it does not have to determine if AI usage occurred.
units.why: The Honor Council asks "is it more likely than not" that unauthorized aid was given and "does not have to determine if AI usage occurred"; a standard of proof, P69.

units.passage: the Honor Council will consider factors including (but not limited to): Assignment instructions Syllabus policies
units.why: The council "will consider factors including" assignment instructions, syllabus policies, comparison with the full body of work, and testimony; kinds of evidence to weigh, P69.

units.passage: The honor council generally will not consider the following factors: AI detection scores Other students’ work in the class (unless there is an allegation of collaboration)
units.why: The council "will not" consider "AI detection scores" among other factors, so detector scores are excluded as evidence; P69 (broadened) rather than P39 because it states what evidence counts in an integrity finding.

units.passage: The OUAI requires human analysis of any work being reported as AI plagiarism, although AI detector evidence may be included in a report.
units.policy: The OUAI requires human analysis of any work being reported as AI plagiarism, although AI detector evidence may be included in a report
units.why: 'The OUAI requires human analysis of any work being reported as AI plagiarism, although AI detector evidence may be included': detector output is only supporting evidence (P69).

units.passage: Reports from AI detection tools may inform your conversations with students regarding inappropriate use of generative AI, but relying solely on detection tools to “catch” someone using AI is likely to lead to ineffective and stressful interactions with students.
units.why: 'Reports from AI detection tools may inform your conversations with students' makes detector output supporting information, not proof (P69).

units.passage: the Office for Undergraduate Academic Integrity does not accept AI detection reports as a form of evidence for Honor Code cases.
units.why: 'the Office for Undergraduate Academic Integrity does not accept AI detection reports as a form of evidence' sets an evidence standard (P69).

units.passage: Faculty should remain professional, objective and focused on the observed behavior and available information.
units.why: 'Faculty should remain professional, objective and focused on the observed behavior' sets an evidence-based stance toward suspected misuse; P69 fits only partly since it names no standard of proof.
units.fit_note: Asks for objectivity and reliance on observed behavior; sets no standard of proof or list of acceptable evidence. / Asks for objectivity but states no evidence standard.

units.passage: Avoid making assumptions before reviewing all available information
units.policy: Faculty and staff are encouraged to avoid making assumptions before reviewing all available information.
units.why: 'Avoid making assumptions before reviewing all available information' guards against premature conclusions in suspected cases; close to P69 but sets no evidence standard.
units.fit_note: Asks for review of all information before judging; no standard of proof is set. / Procedural caution, not a standard of proof.

units.passage: The Honor System Advisory Committee should convene a working group to address potential language changes in the current Honor Code, and to consider whether it is feasible to draft a framework to determine how to access whether AI has been used to reach the threshold of proof — beyond a reasonable doubt
units.why: The working group should consider a framework 'to determine how to access whether AI has been used to reach the threshold of proof', which sets evidence standards for AI misuse findings, P69.

units.passage: Integrate AI-specific scenarios into Honor Code training and case procedures, ensuring that any investigation of potential violations involves multiple forms of evidence and maintains a consistent burden of proof required similar to other violations.
units.why: 'ensuring that any investigation of potential violations involves multiple forms of evidence and maintains a consistent burden of proof' sets evidence standards, P69.

units.passage: William & Mary currently employs only one standard—beyond a reasonable doubt. Crucially, schools like Hamilton College and UVA explicitly caution against relying solely on AI detectors like Turnitin’s AI writing indicator, citing high false-positive rates and equity concerns. Instead, detectors are treated as preliminary tools that must be paired with qualitative evidence and contextual analysis to reach the threshold of proof. To evaluate whether a student used AI without authorization, universities increasingly rely on textual indicators and writing analysis.
units.why: 'William & Mary currently employs only one standard—beyond a reasonable doubt' states the Honor Council's current burden of proof for misuse, P69.

units.passage: Best practice: Use multiple red flags in combination, not any one sign, to build a strong case.
units.why: 'Best practice: Use multiple red flags in combination, not any one sign, to build a strong case' (a peer-institution summary) states what counts as enough evidence, P69.
units.fit_note: Summarizes practice at peer institutions in an appendix, not a W&M rule.

units.passage: AI-Detection Tools • Role: Preliminary indicator, not standalone proof. • Thresholds: Low Reliability: Tools like GPTZero or Copyleaks require corroboration (e.g., Turnitin’s 0.8+ confidence score). High Reliability: Only admissible if the tool is institutionally vetted (e.g., Liberty University’s Turnitin policy). 2.
units.why: Framework: AI-detection tools have a 'Role: Preliminary indicator, not standalone proof' - detector output as support only (P69); admin, when-misuse, should.

units.passage: Confirm the course’s AI policy was clearly communicated in the syllabus.
units.why: 'Confirm the course's AI policy was clearly communicated in the syllabus' is a first step in the sample decision framework, a condition for finding misuse (P69).
units.fit_note: Makes a communicated syllabus policy a precondition for any finding. / Used as a check at the start of an investigation rather than as a duty on instructors.

units.passage: False-Positive Mitigation: Exclude non-native English speakers’ work from detector-heavy evaluations.
units.why: 'Exclude non-native English speakers' work from detector-heavy evaluations' guards against detector bias; P69 (evidence standards) is nearest.
units.fit_note: Names a specific bias safeguard: leave non-native speakers' work out of detector-heavy evaluations. / Excludes a group from detector-heavy evaluation to reduce bias rather than setting a proof standard.
